about: The structured source of the methods and literature page (PLAN.md D72). Every text is copied word for word from the lane dossier under docs/research/ or from docs/research/BACKLOG.md; every number of ours is copied from the report it names. export/research_methods.py checks both before it writes methods.json into a site data root, and reads experiment results from the files named under results.

foundations.cite: Chang, Maheswaran, Su, Kwok, Levy, Wexler, Squire. Quantifying Shot Quality in the NBA. MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference 2014 (research paper competition).
foundations.take: Shot quality as the make probability of a league-average shooter from SportVU features (location, defender distance, more), scored by MSE (Brier) under cross-validation. We use the same idea and the same feature family, but our model adds a shooter prior, so it is not a league-average-player quantity, and we select by log loss with folds grouped by game.

foundations.cite: Zadrozny, Elkan. Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates. KDD 2002, pp. 694-699.
foundations.take: Isotonic regression (pool adjacent violators) as a calibrator for any ranking score; the paper notes PAV "overfits slightly the training data" but beats sigmoid fitting (Section 5 results). Ours fits it on inner out-of-fold scores grouped by game and adds an ad hoc clip to [0.02, 0.98].

foundations.cite: Vovk, Petej. Venn-Abers predictors. UAI 2014.
foundations.take: Venn predictors built on isotonic regression: each test object gets two probabilities (p0, p1), and under IID data one of them, selected by the true label, is perfectly calibrated (Theorem 1). Not used yet; it is the basis of xfg-E1.

foundations.cite: Vovk, Petej, Fedorova. Large-scale probabilistic predictors with and without guarantees of validity. NeurIPS 2015.
foundations.take: Inductive and cross Venn-Abers predictors (IVAP, CVAP) and the log-loss minimax merge p = GM(p1) / (GM(1 - p0) + GM(p1)) (Section 4). Section 5.2 shows plain isotonic regression can give infinite log loss when a test score falls outside the calibration scores; our clip is the kind of ad hoc fix the authors decline to use. Not used yet; xfg-E1.

The lane takes the shooter of an attempt from the play-by-play name matched to the tracking roster, and the names that fail are not random (two players with one short name, a later name, mojibake, a suffix). When the name does not resolve, the lane takes the player nearest the ball at release as the shooter (analytics/xfg/features.py, lines 30 to 31 and 273 to 275). In the training games 5477 out-of-fold attempts did not resolve by name: 5079 took the player nearest the ball, for the shooter prior and the contest features, and 398 had no shooter and so no contest features. Another 611 tracked attempts carry a name that fits two teammates and went to the first of them (reports/export/name_joins.json). The lane was not refit (PLAN.md D94, D95); the site withholds the shot-making values those joins touch.

experiments.title: cross Venn-Abers calibration for a per-shot interval (the pilot)
experiments.what: cross Venn-Abers in place of the inner isotonic step
experiments.hypothesis: Replacing the frozen inner isotonic step of hgb_contest_prior by a cross Venn-Abers predictor (CVAP) on the same three inner folds keeps log loss (non-inferior) and gives every shot an interval (p0, p1); the log-minimax merge replaces the [0.02, 0.98] clip.
experiments.threshold: Adopt CVAP as the calibrator if the paired difference in log loss (CVAP merged minus frozen isotonic) has a 95 percent upper bound of at most +0.0005 on development games, and again on the D71 test set when scored once. +0.0005 is under 1.5 percent of the 0.037 contest gain. Separately, the site copy rule is fixed now: if the 95th percentile of p1 - p0 is under 0.01, the site states xFG as a point estimate whose calibration step moves it by under 0.01; otherwise each shot shows its (p0, p1).
experiments.backlog_status: done: not adopted (passed on development games, inconclusive on the 10-game test set; reports/research/xfg-E1.md)

foundations.cite: Maheswaran, Chang, Henehan, Danesis. Deconstructing the Rebound with Optical Tracking Data. MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference 2012.
foundations.take: SportVU positions of players and ball around a miss; offensive rebound rate depends non-linearly on shot location; which team rebounds becomes more predictable as the ball falls (Section 7). We predict the player, not the team, at one moment (the rim frame).

foundations.cite: Maheswaran, Chang, Su, Kwok, Levy, Wexler, Hollingsworth. The Three Dimensions of Rebounding. MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference 2014.
foundations.take: Rebounding as positioning at the shot, crash to the rim, then conversion; the value of a player's Voronoi cell, weighted by where similar misses land, is re-evaluated at the moment the ball is closest to the rim (Sections 3 and 4). Our rim frame matches their crash endpoint; we learn the probability from features instead of integrating a landing map over Voronoi cells.

foundations.cite: Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017.
foundations.take: Temperature scaling, a one-parameter recalibration that keeps the ranking. Our tau is that idea applied to log q within each miss; top-1 is unchanged by it (reports/archive/rebounds.md).

foundations.cite: Cao, Qin, Liu, Tsai, Li. Learning to rank: from pairwise approach to listwise approach. ICML 2007, pp. 129-136.
foundations.take: A listwise loss built from probability models over the whole list of objects. Our model does not use it: it trains on single candidate rows. rebounds-E2 trains on the whole miss in this listwise way.

foundations.cite: Chen, Guestrin. XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System. KDD 2016.
foundations.take: Tree boosting on first and second order gradient statistics of the loss (Section 2.2), so any twice-differentiable loss, including a within-miss softmax, can be boosted. The tool for rebounds-E2.

foundations.cite: Franks, A., Miller, A., Bornn, L., Goldsberry, K. (2015). Characterizing the spatial structure of defensive skill in professional basketball. Annals of Applied Statistics 9(1), 94-121.
foundations.take: Two things. (1) Matchups: a hidden Markov model where the defender's position is normal around a convex mix of attacker, ball and hoop, mean = 0.62 O + 0.11 B + 0.27 H estimated by EM, stable across 100 games fitted on 30 possessions each, with transition parameter 0.96 to 0.99 (section 3). Ours fixes the weights by hand (attacker plus half the attacker-basket midpoint) and has no transition model. (2) Defensive skill: outcomes split into shot frequency by court region and shot efficiency, with hierarchical shrinkage; 2013-14 SportVU, half-court possessions of at least 5 s, up to the first shot. Ours regresses possession points directly.

foundations.cite: Franks, A. M., D'Amour, A., Cervone, D., Bornn, L. (2016). Meta-analytics: tools for understanding the statistical properties of sports metrics. Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 12(4), 151-165.
foundations.take: Stability (does the metric measure the same thing over time), discrimination (does it separate players) and independence. Our defender table was never checked for stability; this paper gives the frame for that check.

foundations.cite: Keshri, S., Oh, M., Zhang, S., Iyengar, G. (2019). Automatic event detection in basketball using HMM with energy based defensive assignment. Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 15(2), 141-153.

foundations.take: The canonical defender position as a convex mix of attacker, ball and hoop (section 3): the idea that a defender's distance has an expected part set by the ball and the basket. Ours models the nearest defender's distance with no assignment and a linear expectation.

foundations.cite: Keshri, S., Oh, M., Zhang, S., Iyengar, G. (2019). Automatic event detection in basketball using HMM with energy based defensive assignment. Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 15(2), 141-153.
foundations.take: A player- and location-dependent attraction model, which is a model-based form of gravity built into the assignment. Ours is a residual of a location-only expectation. Full text not read; nothing beyond the abstract is used.

foundations.cite: Barron, B., Sitaraman, N., Arias, T. (2025). Analyzing NBA player positions and interactions with density-functional fluctuation theory. Scientific Reports 15, 19830.
foundations.take: Gravity as the change in local defensive density a specific player causes, compared with a typical player at the same spot and with the same teammate positions, so the pull of the other four attackers is removed ("Player gravity" section). Gravity is location-specific (eight half-court spots, on and off ball). Data: Second Spectrum, 2022-23 up to 20 January 2023, positions within 3 s before a shot. Ours does not condition on teammates and gives one number per player.

experiments.title: does gravity open shots for teammates?
experiments.what: does gravity open shots for teammates
experiments.hypothesis: a teammate's shot is more open (larger nearest-defender distance at release) when the shooter's on-floor teammates have higher gravity, beyond the shot's location and the shooter.
experiments.threshold: candidate minus baseline MSE below zero with the paired interval excluding zero, and an effect of at least 0.2 ft of openness per standard deviation of teammates' gravity sum. If it fails, the site says gravity was tested against teammates' openness and showed no effect of that size.
experiments.backlog_status: done: not adopted on development (candidate minus baseline MSE -0.0076 [-0.0152, -0.0002] ft squared; effect per SD of teammates' gravity sum 0.0145 [-0.0660, 0.1016] ft, so the pre-registered 0.2 ft is ruled out; Set A was not scored, PLAN.md D109; reports/research/gravity-E1.md)
writeup_notes: That effect is 0.014 ft per SD (95 percent interval -0.066 to 0.102; 62358 attempts in 604 games), so 0.2 lies above the whole interval: for this estimand, an effect of that size is ruled out.

Post hoc and read by no rule: the sum alone, with the maximum not held fixed, gives 0.109 [0.053, 0.167] ft per SD on the same development folds, so a total effect of the sum does not reach 0.2 either; "ruled out" is said of the committed estimand only.
In the dossier's words for a fail: gravity was tested against teammates' openness and showed no effect of that size.
Set A was not scored (PLAN.md D109): under D107 its reading could only stop an adoption, and there is none to stop; at its size it could not separate 0.0145 from zero either.

foundations.cite: Le, H. M., Carr, P., Yue, Y., Lucey, P. (2017). Data-Driven Ghosting using Deep Imitation Learning. MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference, Boston, 3 to 4 March 2017.
foundations.take: The idea of a league-average ghost and of team-specific ghosts by fine-tuning. Theirs: soccer, 100 games, 10 Hz, about 17400 sequences, a two-layer LSTM with 512 units trained with imitation learning to control drift over long rollouts. Ours: basketball, an MLP on 1 s of history, trained on one step only, scored over a 1 s rollout.

foundations.cite: Le, H. M., Yue, Y., Carr, P., Lucey, P. (2017). Coordinated Multi-Agent Imitation Learning. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70:1995-2003.
foundations.take: The training procedure: roll the policy out over a horizon that grows from 1 to 10 steps so that training sees its own errors (section 4.2), and a latent role model for coordination. Theirs: soccer, 45 games, all ten outfield defenders rolled out jointly. Ours: one defender, others actual, no rollout in training.

foundations.cite: Seidl, T., Cherukumudi, A., Hartnett, A., Carr, P., Lucey, P. (2018). Bhostgusters: Realtime Interactive Play Sketching with Synthesized NBA Defenses. MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference.
foundations.take: The basketball version of ghosting: five role LSTMs, trained in three phases (one-step pre-training, single-policy rollout with other players actual, then joint rollout), and ensembles of 10 runs, which had lower error than single models (section 2.3). Ours stops at the first phase.

foundations.cite: Felsen, P., Lucey, P., Ganguly, S. (2018). Where Will They Go? Predicting Fine-Grained Adversarial Multi-Agent Motion using Conditional Variational Autoencoders. ECCV 2018, pp. 732-747.
foundations.take: The closest basketball forecasting setup: predict defenders given the offense's actual future motion, 2015-16 STATS data, 5 Hz. Also: velocity extrapolation is the strong simple baseline, and role alignment helps. Theirs: CVAE, 4 s history, all five defenders jointly. Ours: deterministic MLP, 1 s history, one defender.

That interval excludes the development estimate (-1.295), so D113's reading is "inconsistent", and under D113 that stops the adoption.
Beside it, report only and fixed before the score (D115): the interval's upper end, -1.085, is below -0.10 ft, so on the test games the gain is at least the pre-registered bar.

The report said before the score why the reading could be "inconsistent": the development estimate pools five stand-in refits that differ from one another (fold 3's at 4.266 ft), while Set A scores one.
The rule stands as written.

experiments.title: a held-out style score, split-half and test-set self-retrieval
experiments.what: a first held-out style score by self-retrieval
experiments.hypothesis: the frozen PCA embedding identifies a player's style across disjoint games. Built from one set of games, a player's embedding has their own embedding from other games among its 5 nearest neighbours far more often than chance.
experiments.threshold: the embedding is reported as validated on held-out games if the test-set top-5 self-retrieval rate has the lower end of its 95 percent interval above 0.25 and above the position-only retriever's upper end. foundations.cite: Cervone, D'Amour, Bornn, Goldsberry (2014). POINTWISE: Predicting Points and Valuing Decisions in Real Time with NBA Optical Tracking Data. MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference, Research Paper Competition.
foundations.take: The definition we use: EPV = E[points to end of possession given the state] (page 2).
foundations.differs: They model the ball handler's next action (pass, shot, turnover as macrotransitions, movement as microtransitions) and sum over futures (page 3, Eq. 1); we regress realized points directly on a state summary. They used 2012-13 data.

foundations.cite: Cervone, D'Amour, Bornn, Goldsberry (2016). A Multiresolution Stochastic Process Model for Predicting Basketball Possession Outcomes. Journal of the American Statistical Association 111(514).
foundations.take: The full model: competing-risk hazards for six macrotransitions, hierarchical spatial shrinkage across players, 25 Hz STATS data from 2013-14, 90/10 split (Sections 2.2, 3.2, 5.1).
foundations.differs: Our model is a direct regression with no transition structure and no player-level spatial effects beyond two priors. They report that without shrinkage the model can do worse than one with no spatial effects (Section 5.1).

foundations.cite: Sicilia, Pelechrinis, Goldsberry (2019). DeepHoops: Evaluating Micro-Actions in Basketball Using Deep Feature Representations of Spatio-Temporal Data. arXiv working paper (secondary indexes list it at KDD 2019; the ACM page was not checked).
foundations.take: Learn from raw positions: a stacked LSTM over 128 moments (about 5 s) of all 10 players and the ball, predicting the terminal action class (shot attempt, shooting foul, non-shooting foul, turnover, null), with expected points as the probability-weighted value of the classes (Sections 3, 4).
foundations.differs: We feed 25 hand features at 1 Hz and predict points directly; they predict terminal classes and attach league-average point values. 2016-17 data, about 750 games.

foundations.cite: Fernandez, Bornn, Cervone (2021). A framework for the fine-grained evaluation of the instantaneous expected value of soccer possessions. Machine Learning (DOI 10.1007/s10994-021-05989-6).
foundations.take: EPV decomposed by the law of total expectation into action selection times expected value given the action, with the shot term equal to an expected-goals model (Section 3.2, Eq. 1 to 4).
foundations.differs: Soccer, not basketball; we use no decomposition and train on realized outcomes, including the make or miss of every shot.

foundations.cite: Alcorn, Nguyen (2021). baller2vec: A Multi-Entity Transformer For Multi-Agent Spatiotemporal Modeling. arXiv preprint.

experiments.title: is the target reliable, and is the metric more than decision mix?
experiments.what: is the target reliable, and is the metric more than decision mix
experiments.hypothesis: (H1) per-player on-court offensive rating, measured per game, has split-half reliability below 0.2 across the development games, so a per-game Spearman with it is close to zero whatever the decision metric does; (H2) the frozen per-player mean quality has a stability (Franks et al., Eq. 4, game-level bootstrap) of at least 0.5; (H3) at least half of the between-player variance of the frozen mean quality is explained by the player's shares of shot, pass and drive decisions.
experiments.threshold: if H1 holds, the lane report adds, next to the unchanged failed verdict, that the frozen validation could not have detected a signal; the kind-adjusted quality replaces the frozen mean in the player table only if its stability is at least 0.5 with the 95 percent interval above 0.3 and its R squared on kind shares is below 0.2. If H1 fails (the target is reliable), the failed verdict is read as evidence against the metric, and that is written down.

protocol.caveat: Post hoc, not pre-registered: stepped down to one game, the target's reliability is about 0.04, which would meet H1's intent; part of the half-season reliability may be team offence shared by teammates (not measured).
not_scored: The pre-registration asks for the same statistics once on the D71 test set. They cannot exist there, so the test set was not touched and the scoring ledger has no decisions-E1 entry.
On one date every team plays once, so every player has at most one game. No player can sit in both halves, so split-half reliability and stability have no player at all.

Discrimination and R squared need 300 decisions in the set. Post hoc: the most decisions any player made in one of the 12769 development player-games is 229 (99th percentile 153). No player can reach 300 in one game.

experiments.title: one value scale for every option, validated on the decisions actually made
experiments.what: one value scale for every option, validated on decisions made
experiments.hypothesis: valuing every option on the EPV scale (POINTWISE, Fernandez et al.) gives values whose chosen-option value predicts the points that followed, which the frozen hand-set values do less well. Option values: shot = points times the out-of-fold xFG probability; pass to teammate j = P(completion to j given the decision frame) times the EPV of a state with j holding the ball at the decision frame, plus P(failure) times 0; drive = P(drive keeps the ball) times the EPV of the state 1 s later on the drive, using the observed drive path only for the chosen drive and a model of that state for an unchosen one; hold = the EPV as now. Completion and drive models are fitted out of fold by game, under tools/.
experiments.threshold: the regret coefficient's 95 percent interval above 0, the paired difference (new minus frozen) in that coefficient with interval above 0, and the chosen-value calibration slope inside 0.8 to 1.2, all on development games. Then scored once on the D71 test set.

foundations.cite: Wiseman, Shieber, Rush. Challenges in Data-to-Document Generation. EMNLP 2017.
foundations.take: RotoWire: NBA box scores to game summaries, scored by extractive metrics (an information extraction model run on the output). Their template system "scores very poorly on BLEU, but does quite well on the extractive metrics" (Section 6.1): relation generation precision 99.30 percent on test against 71.82 for the best neural row (Table 2). genai-E1 asks the same question of our checker. Ours checks every number by rule against the item's own facts, not by a learned extractor, and needs no reference text.

foundations.cite: Thomson, Reiter. A Gold Standard Methodology for Evaluating Accuracy in Data-To-Text Systems. INLG 2020.
foundations.take: Human accuracy annotation: three annotators per text mark each error as "Incorrect number", "Incorrect named entity", "Incorrect word", "Context error", "Not checkable" or "Other", merged by majority (Sections 3.2 to 3.5). Our human faithfulness protocol (genai-E2) uses their categories for what the checker cannot see; our readers are not paid crowd workers, and our texts are about 100 words, not 300.

foundations.cite: Hu et al. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv 2106.09685, 2021.
foundations.take: Freeze the weights and train low-rank matrices in each layer; "on-par or better than fine-tuning" on the models they test, with "no additional inference latency" (abstract). We use it because a 1.5B model cannot be fully fine-tuned in 16 GB.

foundations.cite: Kim, Rush. Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation. EMNLP 2016.
foundations.take: Train the student on the teacher's output sequences; their student "runs 10 times faster than its state-of-the-art teacher with little loss in performance" (abstract, translation). Our A1 arm trains on the Haiku texts, which are also filtered by the checker, so it learns only from passing outputs.

foundations.cite: Yuan et al. Scaling Relationship on Learning Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models. arXiv 2308.01825, 2023.
foundations.take: Rejection sampling fine-tuning: k sampled paths per question, wrong ones filtered by answer and by a Python check, duplicates removed (Section 3); on GSM8K, LLaMA-7B rises from 35.9 (SFT) to 41.7 (RFT, k = 100), and "RFT brings more improvement for less performant LLMs" (abstract, Table 1), while for 33B "RFT does not improve performance compared to SFT". Our A2 is the same loop with our checker as the filter, k = 4.

foundations.cite: Qwen team. Qwen2.5 Technical Report. arXiv 2412.15115, 2024.
foundations.take: The 0.5B and 1.5B open-weight models are Apache 2.0, 32K context with 8K generation (Table 1); the 3B is under the "Qwen Research" license, so it is not used.

experiments.threshold: Paired bootstrap by player (scouting) or by game (possession), 2000 resamples, 95 percent percentile interval of the difference. - H1, training helps: the dev-best fine-tuned arm minus A0, per kind and size. Passes when the difference is at least +0.10 and its lower bound is above 0; fails when the upper bound is below +0.10; otherwise inconclusive. - H2, the checker as a teacher: A2 minus A1. Lower bound above 0: rejection sampling adds to distillation; upper bound below 0: it hurts; otherwise inconclusive. - H3, near the API model (scouting only): the dev-best arm with the repair loop minus Haiku as delivered. Lower bound at or above -0.05: non-inferior; upper bound below -0.05: inferior; otherwise inconclusive. At 81 players the interval half-width of a pass-rate difference is about 0.1 near rates of 0.8, so inconclusive is a likely reading and is stated as such. - H4, constrained decoding: A3 minus its arm, on the number_value failure rate and on the pass rate.
